extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers of classical mechanics and fluid dynamics (readers of a Latin mathematical physics treatise)
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and summarize the distinct theoretical propositions, hypotheses, and corollaries about waves, pulses, sound, and circular fluid motion presented in this Latin textbook excerpt (classical mechanics / fluid dynamics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Isochrony of alternating water motion (Corol. I)
rubrics_metrics.description: Igitur aquae ascendentis & descendentis, sive motus intensior sit sive remissior, vices omnes sunt isochronae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement: the alternating ascents and descents of water (or the alternating motion) are all isochronous — each cycle takes the same time regardless of intensity. Context: follows from the comparison of water column motion to pendulum motion; used to deduce periodic behavior of reciprocating fluid motion. (Q.E.D.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative reciprocity of water/pendulum motions (Corol. 2 & 3 surrounding Prop.XLV/XLVI)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the whole length of water in a channel is a given amount (e.g., so many Parisian feet) then the alternating descent and ascent occur at fixed intervals (examples give numeric feet per second); increasing or decreasing the total water length increases or decreases the reciprocation time in the subduplicate (square-root) ratio of the lengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives applied numeric examples (pendulum lengths and resulting periods) and warns that the proposition assumes parts of water ascend/descend rectilinearly; actual ascent/descent occurs more nearly by circular arcs so the time is only approximate. Used to relate water column length to period by subduplicate ratio (square-root scaling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositio XLV: Undarum velocitas est in subduplicata ratione latitudinum
rubrics_metrics.description: Undarum velocitas est in subduplicata ratione latitudinum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short statement: the velocity of waves is in the subduplicate (square-root) ratio of their transverse measures (latitudines). The text notes this follows from construction in the next proposition. Acts as a compact law relating wave speed to wave amplitude/width (as defined in the text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositio XLVI (Problem X): Construction to measure wave velocity via pendulum
rubrics_metrics.description: Constituatur pendulum cujus longitudo, inter punctum suspensionis & centrum oscillationis, sequetur latitudini undarum: & quo tempore pendulum illud oscillationes singulas peragit, eodem undae progrediendo latitudinem suam propemodum conficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a pendulum whose length is proportional to the wave 'latitudo' so that in the time the pendulum makes a single oscillation the wave advances approximately one of its transverse measures. The proposition defines 'latitudo' as transverse measure between troughs and crests and derives corollaries giving practical numeric speeds (feet per second) for waves of given widths, noting approximation because actual particle paths are circular not rectilinear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositio XLVII (Theorem XXXVII): Particle motion under pulses follows pendulum law
rubrics_metrics.description: Pulsibus per fluidum propagatis, singulce fluidi particulcs, motu reciproco brevissimo euntes & redeuntes, accelerantur semper & retardantur pro lege oscillantis penduli.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement: particles of a fluid subject to propagated pulses accelerate and retard following the same law as an oscillating pendulum. The proof maps time of vibration to arcs on a circle so that each medium particle undergoes accelerations/retardations in the same sequence and proportion as a pendulum; corollary: the number of propagated pulses equals the number of vibrations of the tremulous body (pulses are not multiplied in progression). Detailed geometric construction and proportionality relations provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary to Prop. XLVII: Pulses are not multiplied in propagation
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerus pulsuum propagatorum idem sit cum numero vibrationum corporis tremuli, neque multiplicatur in eorum progressu.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a medium line-element returns to its first place and rests, it will not move further unless driven by new impulse; thus pulses cease when source ceases. This explains why sounds stop almost immediately when the generating motion stops (especially at distance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositio XLVIII (Theorem XXXVIII): Pulse velocity depends on elasticity and density
rubrics_metrics.description: Pulsuum in fluido elastico propagatorum velocitates sunt in ratione composita ex subduplicata ratione vis elasticae directe & subduplicata ratione densitatis inverse; si modo fluidi vis elastica ejusdem condensationi proportionalis esse supponatur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives derivation and treats cases: (1) homogeneous media with equal pulse distances => equal propagation speeds; (2) different pulse lengths in different media but corresponding parts undergo proportionate contractions/dilations leading to equal driving elastic forces; (3) if elastic force and density equal among media then pulses are all equally fast. Final formula: pulse speed ~ sqrt(vis_elastica / densitas) (i.e., subduplicate direct in elastic force and subduplicate inverse in density).

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositio XLIX (Problem XI): Compute pulse speed from medium density and elasticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Datis inedii densitate & vi elastica, invenire velocitatem pulsum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct an equivalent pendulum: choose a pendulum length A equal to the altitude of a homogeneous medium whose weight equals the incumbent pressure and whose density matches the compressed medium. The pulse propagates the circumference equivalent to that radius A in the time corresponding to the pendulum oscillation; corollary: pulse speed equals the speed acquired by gravity falling through half the altitude A. Also corollary: since A is proportional to elastic force and inversely to density, pulse velocity is in combined ratio subduplicate(density^{-1}) and subduplicate(elastic_force). Includes numeric example and physical considerations (effect of particle size, vapours, temperature) for sound speed in air with computed numerical values and corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositio L (Problem XII): Determination of pulse wavelengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporis, cujus tremore pulsu excitantur, inveniatur numerus vibrationum dato tempore. Per numerum illum dividatur spatium quod pulsu eodem tempore percurrere possit, & pars inventa erit pulsus unius latitudo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given the number of oscillations a source makes in a time interval and the distance a pulse travels in that time, divide the distance by the number of vibrations to obtain the pulse (wavelength) width. Scholium links these propositions to light and sound: sound as air-pulses and quantitative discussion of sound speeds, experimental data (Sauvetier's flute experiment), and environmental corrections (humidity, vapors, temperature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium: Sound as air pulses and practical corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Soni sunt aeris pulsi propagati; speed computations use specific weights and barometer heights; effects of particulate size, vapours, and temperature modify numeric sound speed (examples compute feet per second for London/Paris and corrections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed numerical derivation: relates densities (air, rainwater, mercury), barometer readings, and produces estimated speeds (e.g., ~1142 London feet per second, ~1070 Parisian feet) with corrections for particulate thickness and vapours; notes seasonal variation (faster in summer, slower in winter) via subduplicate dependence on density and elasticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (Sectio IX): Resistance proportional to separation speed
rubrics_metrics.description: Resistentiam, qucs oritur ex defectu lubricitatis partium fluidi, ceteris paribus, proportionalem esse velocitati, qua partes fluidi separantur ab invicem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypothesis used in ensuing propositions on circular motion of fluids: resistance due to lack of lubricity (mutual friction) is proportional to the velocity at which parts of the fluid separate from each other (linear viscous-type assumption).

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositio LI (Theorem XXXIX): Circular motion in fluid driven by rotating cylinder — periods ∝ distance from axis
rubrics_metrics.description: Si cylindrus solidus infinite longus in fluido uniformi & infinito circa axem positione datum uniformi cum motu revolvatur ... dico quod tempora periodica partium fluidi sunt ut ipsarum distantiae ab axe cylindri.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an infinite cylinder rotates in an infinite uniform fluid and each fluid part preserves uniform circular motion, the periodic times of fluid particles are proportional to their distances from the cylinder axis (i.e., angular velocities inversely proportional to radius; absolute tangential velocities equal). Corollaries treat nested cylinders, addition of common angular motion, propagation of rotation through fluid, and qualitative experimental remarks (observable in deep water). The proof uses balance of applied impressed translations and surfaces and limiting process to continuous medium and hyperbolic-area arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollaries to Prop. LI: consequences for concentric cylinders and added motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Corol. 1: angular motions inversely as distances, absolute velocities equal. Corol. 2–6: behavior when inner/outer cylinders rotate, propagation of motion through fluid, conservation/dissipation when outer cylinder restrained, and acceleration of outer cylinder if allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These corollaries specify how imposed rotation on an inner cylinder is communicated through a concentric fluid to outer regions, how adding/subtracting a common angular motion does not change mutual friction relations, and how the system responds if outer cylinder is held or freed; includes experimental suggestion that these effects can be observed in deep water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositio LII (Theorem XL): Circular motion driven by rotating sphere — periods ∝ square(distance from center)
rubrics_metrics.description: Si sphaera solida, in fluido uniformi & infinito, circa axem positione datum uniformi cum motu revolvatur ... dico quod tempora periodica partium fluidi erunt ut quadrata distantiarum a centro sphaerae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a solid sphere rotates in an infinite uniform fluid and each fluid element maintains uniform circular motion, the periodic times of fluid particles are proportional to the square of their distances from the sphere's center (i.e., angular velocities scale with inverse-square of radius; derived via translation/surface proportionality arguments and limiting sums leading to hyperbolic-area/quadrature relations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollaries to Prop. LII: implications for vortices and conservation
rubrics_metrics.description: Cor. 1–9: angular motions of fluid particles about sphere's axis vary as inverse squares of distances; rotating sphere imparts vorticity propagating outward; to maintain a steady vortex requires active input; interactions of multiple vortices and spheres described; final corollaries give necessary conditions for permanent vortex structures in contained vessels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed consequences include: propagation of motion to infinity, transfer of motion from inner to outer fluid preserving total motion, need for continual active principle to conserve vortex, behavior when other spheres are present (inducing secondary vortices), and conditions for permanent vortex in closed spherical vessel. Emphasizes mechanical conservation and dissipative tendencies if applied forces cease.
